A notice for tender was issued by the Executive Engineer on the 23rd of November, 1972 in respect of several items of work including one for re-excavation of a Khal and the date for submission of tender was fixed on the 8th of December, 1972. Eleven tenders were received for the aforesaid work and the lowest quotation was 45% above the estimated costs and thereafter a comparative statement of the quotations received along with the tenders were sent by the Executive Engineer to the Superintending Engineer, Dacca Irrigation Circle, on the 10th of December, 1972 for consideration by the Tender Board. The Superintending Engineer thereafter informed the Executive Engineer that the rates having been considered high, attempts should he made for lowering the rate by negotiation. Thereafter the Executive Engineer is stated to have persuaded the Contractors to accept the work at the reduced rate and re-submitted the tenders to the Superintending Engineer by his Memo. dated the 5th of January, 1973. The Tender Board accepted the said negotiated rate for the work and communicated its decision to the petitioner under Chief Engineer's Memo dated the 8th of January 1973, on receipt of the said decision of the Tender Board, the Executive Engineer by his Memo. dated 15.1.73 informed the Contractors of the approval of the rate by the Chief Engine and requested them to execute the formal agreement within a week from the date and thereafter to contact the Sub-Divisional Engineer, Irrigation, Gopalganj for detailed work order for the execution of the work. It is stated in the petition that the Contractors did not immediately call at the office of the Executive Engineer to execute the formal agreement after receipt of the Executive Engineer's intimation and that nine out of the ten Contractors executed the formal agreement on 13.2.73 whereupon the Executive Engineer issued a Memo to the Sub-Divisional Engineer (Irrigation), Gopalganj on the 14th of February, 1973 requesting him to issue detailed work order to the Contractors immediately. The Sub-Divisional Engineer was also asked to see that the defaulting Contractor namely, Mr. S. A. Mannan might sign the agreement without further delay. The Sub-Divisional Engineer (Irrigation) Gopalganj issued detailed work order then and there, on receipt of the aforesaid Memo, to the Contractors in question allowing each of them two months' time to complete the work. It is further stated in the petition that the Executive Engineer as well as the Sub-Divisional Engineer having found the progress of work unsatisfactory in certain cases, asked the Contractors by a letter dated the 20th March, 1973 to increase labour strength so as to complete the week in time according to schedule. 

 8. It has also been alleged in the petition that there has been malafide on the part of the Respondent No. 2 in respect of the order passed inasmuch as the Respondent No. 2 used to bear some grudge as against the Executive Engineer. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the Respondents in which it is stated that there have been unnecessary delay in issuing the detailed work order due to the laches of the officers concerned and their subordinate staff at Gopalganj and also lack of supervision on their part which caused delay in the execution of the work. It is further stated that the alleged completion of 80% of the work much beyond the scheduled time, can not be said to be at all satisfactory. The case sought to be made out in the affidavit-in-opposition is that the order of suspension and the enquiry ordered by Respondent No. 2 is on the basis of the report of the Prime Minister's Vigilance and Inspection Bureau. The allegation of malafide has been denied and it is maintained that the order of suspension as well as the enquiry has been made strictly in compliance with the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1960. It has further been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that by the order dated the 4th of October, 1973 an opinion has been formed for starting a departmental proceeding and Mr. Mohsinuddin, Project Director, G. K. Project, has been appointed as Enquiry Officer in the said proceeding against the officers concerned. 

 "Whereas it has been brought to the notice of this Ministry that there are serious allegations involving irregularities in connection with excavation work of a Khal from Gopalganj to Kathika julia to Ghagore P.S. Katalipara and also allegations of negligence of official duties which amounts to misconduct against (1) Mr. S. M. Saleh, Executive Engineer, Faridpur Irrigation Division, (2) Mr. M. A. Mannan, S.D.E. (S.A.E.) Irrigation, Gopalganj, (3) Mr. Md. Mahtabuddin, Sectional Officer, Mr. Mohsinuddin, Project Director, Ganges Kobadak Project Phase II, Kushtia is hereby appointed inquiry officer for this case and he is asked to hold necessary enquiry into the above allegation and to submit a report to the Ministry within a month. A statement of facts containing certain serious allegations are enclosed herewith." 

 11. Mr. M. M. Haque, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the Respondents has on the other hand submitted that there are clear allegations of irregularities in the report of the Prime Minister's Vigilance and Inspection Bureau and these irregularities being of the nature, of negligence amount to, in reality, misconduct and as such the authority concerned was perfectly within its powers to draw up the proceeding and place the officers concerned under suspension in accordance with Rule 10 of the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1960.

 Rule 4 enumerated the kinds of penalty, major as well as minor, which may be imposed in keeping with the gravity of the offence, against the officer concerned. In this connection it is also necessary to point out that there are two kinds of enquiry provided in two different Rules, viz. Rule 6 and Rule 6A. Where the allegation is of inefficiency or misconduct calling for minor penalties the procedure as said down in Rule 6 shall have to be followed but in cases of inefficiency, misconduct and corruption calling for major penalties, the procedure as laid down in Rule 6A is to be followed : 

 14. On a consideration of these rules it is clear that when the authority is to make up its mind as to the starting of an enquiry against a certain person. It will have to decide at the same time also as to the nature of the allegations constituting the offence, that is to say, whether the allegations constituting the offence call for major penalties or for minor penalties. A person who is guilty of misconduct may be visited with major penalties or minor penalties according to the nature of the offence charged against him. The instruction No. 2 (Annexure J) as has been framed by the Government in order to give erect to the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, relates to the circumstances under which a Government Servant may be placed under suspension and it is stated there in that no Government servant should be placed under suspension except when this is really necessary. Certain circumstances have been enumerated in the said instruction under which an order of suspension may be made. It is clearly stated therein that no one should be suspended for petty breach of discipline or for minor departmental offences, and no order of suspension should be made unless— 

 16. On an analysis of the facts which have preceded the passing of the order of suspension it does not appear to us that there has been any application of mind by Respondent No. 2 in respect of the said aspect of the case. The allegations were first made in an unsigned petition about corruption of the officers concerned an inquiry was held thereafter by the prime Minister's Vigilance and Inspection Bureau  which came to the definite conclusion that there  was not evidence of corruption, but they were of the view that there had been delay in execution of the project on account of certain irregularities and lack of supervision, without particularising the nature of the irregularity or want of supervision as against any particular officer. There has been a further enquiry by the senior-most officer in the Department namely the Chief Engineer who completely exonerated the officers concerned in respect of the charges of irregularities and lack of supervision. The Respondent No. 2 appears to have had before him both the reports of the Prime Minister's Vigilance and Inspection Bureau as well as of the Chief Engineer. Although in the affidavit in-opposition no reference has been made to the Chief Engineer's report but it has been submitted by the learned Assistant Attorney General that both the reports received due consideration of Respondent No. 2. It may be quite probable that Respondent No. 2 passed the order after reading both the reports. But that is not enough for sustaining the order of suspension passed by the said Respondent if it does appear that there has been absolutely no application of mind to the said reports and also to the other relevant facts. From the order dated the 4th October, it does not appear that Respondent No. 2 did at all pay any consideration to the findings arrived at by the Chief Engineer and the reasoning’s given by him in support of the said findings. So far as Respondent No. 2 is concerned, the Chief Engineer's Report seems to be absolutely non-existent. Furthermore, Respondent No.2 is perfectly within his powers after proper consideration to reject the Chief Engineer's report and to come to his own decision on the basis of his own reasoning’s. But when a public duty has been placed upon him to do a very responsible job for the purpose of maintaining discipline in the service he is required under law to discharge his duty and exercise his discretion after proper consideration of all matters as enjoined under law. 

 17. The Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules and also the instructions in connection therewith make it perfectly cleat that the authority concerned must fist come to grips with the concrete allegations as against a particular officer, constituting the offence. Secondly, he is to come to a definite conclusion whether major penalties or minor penalties are going to be inflicted upon the officer if the allegations are proved and thirdly, he will have to come to a further conclusion that whether in his opinion the suspension is necessary or expedient as has been made clear in Rule 10. The proviso it Rule 10 has also made it clear that in a case where suspension is necessary, he will have to further consider whether the same object will be achieved by asking the officer in question to proceed on leave instead of placing him under suspension. The instruction issued by the Government has also made it abundantly clear that no one should be suspended unless he comes under any of the categories mentioned in the said instruction No. 2. 

 18. It has been laid down in a number of judicial authorities that where a public duty is cast upon certain persons to do an act by exercise of their discretion and there has been no application of mind to the relevant facts before doing the act or it has been done on extra us consideration, it cannot be said that discretion in has at all been exercised in doing the act. reference may be made to the observation of Lord Esher, M. R. made in the case of The Queen Vs. Vestry of St. Pancras, 1890) 24, Queen's Bench, 371, which was to the following effect : 

 19. It has been pointed out by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of the Province of East Pakistan, and another Vs. Jagesh Chandra Lodh and other in 11 DLR (S.C) 411, while considering the question of the validity of an order of requisition passed under The East Bengal (emergency) Requisition of property Act, 1748; that when the government officer did not apply his mind to the question whether it was necessary or expedient to requisition the property for public purpose as required under the law, the order has no legal validity. 

 20. In this case also it seems to us that Respondent No. 2 did not apply his mind at all to the facts and circumstances which he was required to do under the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules as well as Government instructions issued in connection with such matters. On a consideration of the facts it is clear that Respondent No. 2 did not base his decision of suspending the petitioners on matters which the rules relevant to this case enjoined upon him to do and as such it can be said that in the eye of law there has absolutely been no exercise of discretion on his pert. 

 The result, therefore, is that the Rules are made absolute the impugned order of suspension an contained in Annexure 'H' in both the petitions are set aside. The respondents shall pay the costs in both the petitions, the hearing fee being assessed at 15 Gold Mohurs in each case.
